title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
authors: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB
population: Participants in 25 randomised controlled trials of exercise-based sports injury prevention; 26,610 participants with 3,464 injuries
findings: 25 trials with 26,610 participants and 3,464 injuries were analysed; the overall effect estimate was heterogeneous and 12 studies were adjusted for clustering.
Strength training RR 0.315 (0.207-0.480); proprioception training RR 0.550 (0.347-0.869); multiple-exposure programs RR 0.655 (0.520-0.826).

Acute injuries RR 0.647 (0.502-0.836) and overuse injuries RR 0.527 (0.373-0.746) were reduced; authors state strength training reduced sports injuries to less than one third and overuse injuries could be almost halved.
limitations: General sports population, not running-specific; heterogeneous overall effect; the strength-training stratum is a subgroup with a very large point estimate that is likely overstated; the single large running RCT in this corpus (Toresdahl 2020) found no effect.
implications: Include strength work in every plan, but do not quote RR 0.315 as a running-specific injury guarantee.
Do not prescribe static stretching as an injury-prevention measure.
Treat the overuse benefit (RR about 0.53) as supportive only and rely on load-progression rules as the primary injury control.

verification.notes: Crossref year 2013 (online-first), Europe PMC 2014. Removed the researcher's unsupported 'mostly team and ball sports' descriptor, which is not in the abstract.
